questions.q: What does a test's `severity` default to, and what does changing it to `warn` do?
options: It defaults to `error` (a failure stops the build); `warn` reports the failure without stopping anything
It defaults to `warn`; there is no way to make a test block a build
Severity has no effect on whether a build stops
It defaults to `error`, and `warn` deletes the test entirely
questions.explain: Every test is `error` severity by default. Downgrading to `warn` reports the failure (visible in the Test Status lens) without failing the build or the CI check.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when should a test use `error` versus `warn`?
options: `error` for violations that mean the data is definitively wrong; `warn` for things worth a human's attention that aren't automatically a broken pipeline
Every test should always be `error`, with no exceptions
Every test should always be `warn`, so nothing ever blocks a deploy
Severity should be chosen at random to test both code paths
questions.explain: Reserving error for genuine breakage (like a duplicate primary key) and warn for advisory checks keeps a failing test meaningful instead of training a team to ignore red checks.

questions.explain: equal_rowcount compares row counts between two models, catching a transformation that unexpectedly dropped or duplicated rows.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say source freshness checks catch a problem that `not_null`/`unique` tests structurally cannot?
options: Those tests check the data that IS there; freshness checks whether new data has stopped arriving at all, which stale-but-valid rows would pass
Freshness checks are just a slower version of not_null with no real difference
not_null and unique tests already check data freshness automatically
Freshness checks only work on seed files, not real sources
questions.explain: Stale rows that are already loaded are still perfectly valid, non-null data — only a freshness check comparing the newest row's age against a threshold catches an upstream pipeline that silently stopped.

questions.q: In a real freshness config with `warn_after: {count: 12, period: hour}` and `error_after: {count: 24, period: hour}`, what happens if the source hasn't updated in 20 hours?
options: It reports a warning, since 20 hours has passed the warn_after threshold but not yet the error_after threshold
Nothing happens until exactly 24 hours have passed, with no intermediate state
It immediately errors, since any staleness at all is treated as an error
Freshness checks ignore any duration under 48 hours
questions.explain: 20 hours exceeds the 12-hour warn_after threshold but is still under the 24-hour error_after threshold, so `dbt source freshness` reports a warning.
